newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-F.A. DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER PORTO CUP CLASHES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-F.A. DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER PORTO CUP CLASHES.

text.p: The English Football Association (F.A.) said on Thursday it was "deeply concerned" by reports Portuguese police opened fire on Manchester United fans with anti-riot pellets after Wednesday's European Cup match in Oporto.

"Key questions need to be answered quickly," F.A. spokesman David Davies told a news conference in London. "Why did the problems arise? Why were what appear to have been plastic pellets fired at supporters? Who, if anyone, ordered that they should be used?"
He said the F.A. had been in touch with United and the British Foreign Office throughout the day and that Manchester police had discussed Wednesday's incidents with their Portuguese counterparts.
Eight United fans were taken to hospital with pellet wounds after the quarter-final second leg tie against Porto. They were all allowed home early on Thursday morning.

Another 20 or so English fans were slightly hurt in the clashes in which police used batons and threw smoke grenades after a number of United fans ignored police orders and tried to leave the ground before the final whistle.
UEFA said the incident would top the agenda at a committee meeting next Tuesday.
F.A. chief executive Graham Kelly stopped short of blaming Portuguese police for the incidents, but said he was distressed at their use of anti-riot pellets.
"We're unhappy, certainly, that (the fans) were fired upon, we're unhappy with the fact there were injuries.
"I'd be very surprised indeed if there was any suggestion that Manchester United had failed in their responsibilities."
Oporto police denied they had used excessive force. A police chief said no arrests were made and 18 officers had been injured in the incidents, none of them seriously.
Around 10,000 United fans were in Porto's stadium during the match and, as a security precaution, police ordered them to stay there until local fans had left the ground.

It was unclear why United fans ignored the call and tried to force open an exit door but one theory is they suddenly sensed the potential for a crush like the one which killed 96 fans at Hillsborough stadium in Sheffield, northern England, in 1989.
The spectre of Britain's worst ever stadium disaster still hangs over British soccer and Kelly acknowledged it could have been a factor.
"It's right that we remember Hillsborough and it's right we take every measure possible to present a similar occurrence," he said.
Wednesday's match ended 0-0 but Manchester United went through 4-0 on aggregate to become the firsnglish side to reach the last four of the European Cup since 1985.
That was the year Liverpool reached the ill-fated final in the Heysel stadium where 39 Juventus fans died.
